title: Acids, bases and neutralisation

match.reason: No bank point covers the pH scale with 7 as neutral, and the bank cards are written at Year 11 and 12 chemistry depth with extra content such as carbonates, enthalpy and exothermic heat, so none matches this Year 10 point.

draft.title: Acids, bases and neutralisation
card: The pH scale shows how acidic or basic a solution is. A pH below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic, and exactly 7 is neutral.
Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base. It makes a salt and water. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide make sodium chloride and water.
As a base is added to an acid, the pH rises towards 7. As an acid is added to a base, the pH falls towards 7.
A neutralisation reaction can be used to treat acidic soil. A farmer can spread lime, which is a base, to raise the soil pH.
draft.remember: Acid + base makes salt + water, and the pH moves towards 7.

a.q: Which pair of products forms when an acid reacts with a base?
a.why: Neutralisation always makes a salt and water. A metal and hydrogen is made when some metals react with acids, not when a base is used.
a.clue: Think of hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide making table salt.

b.q: Priya's garden soil has a pH of 5. She spreads lime, a base, on it. What is the most likely pH afterwards?
b.why: The soil is acidic and the base partly neutralises it, so the pH rises towards 7. A fall to 3.5 would make it more acidic, which is the wrong direction.
b.clue: Adding a base moves the pH towards 7.

problems.detail: 'As a base is added to an acid, the pH rises towards 7' and the remember line 'the pH moves towards 7' suggest the pH stops at 7. Adding excess base takes the pH above 7. This could mislead students into thinking the pH can never pass 7.
Why (a) says neutralisation 'always' makes a salt and water. The card only says it makes a salt and water. 'Always' overstates this: ammonia and an acid, for example, form only an ammonium salt.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer (salt and water; pH 6.5). Two minor issues: the card and remember line imply the pH stops at 7 when a base is added, and why (a) says 'always'.

proposal.title: Acids, bases and neutralisation
card: The pH scale shows how acidic or basic a solution is. A pH below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic, and exactly 7 is neutral.
Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base. It makes a salt and water. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide make sodium chloride and water.
Adding a base to an acid raises the pH. With just the right amount the pH reaches 7, and extra base takes it above 7. Adding an acid to a base lowers the pH in the same way.
Neutralisation can be used to treat acidic soil. A farmer can spread lime, which is a base, to raise the soil pH.
proposal.remember: Acid + base makes a salt and water. A base raises the pH and an acid lowers it.

a.q: Which pair of products forms when an acid reacts with a base?
a.why: Neutralisation makes a salt and water, as when hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide make sodium chloride and water. A salt and hydrogen gas is tempting, but hydrogen forms when some metals react with acids, not in neutralisation with a base.
a.clue: Recall what hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide make.

b.q: Priya's garden soil has a pH of 5. She spreads lime, a base, on it. What is the most likely pH afterwards?
b.why: A pH of 5 is acidic. Lime neutralises some of the acid, so the pH rises, and 6.5 is the only option above 5. A pH of 3.5 or 4.5 would mean the soil became more acidic, which is the wrong direction.
b.clue: Does adding a base raise or lower the pH?
